qs.q: What is the specific course code assigned to the Chemical Pathology course unit within the Year Three MBChB curriculum?
qs.e: The Chemical Pathology course unit is designated with the course code MBPA 3600 under Human Pathology. Other codes are incorrect distractors not listed in the curriculum details.
qs.s: Department Of Pathology — Course Outline: MCQs

qs.q: What is the main purpose of the Chemical Pathology course unit as outlined in the curriculum?
o: To perform surgical excisions and biopsies
To study gross anatomical structures of organs
To interpret tests for disease diagnosis and management
To analyze microscopic cellular changes in tissue samples
qs.e: Chemical pathology involves the study and application of chemical processes to measure body fluid components for interpreting tests in disease diagnosis. Surgical excisions and gross anatomy belong to other branches of pathology.
qs.s: Department Of Pathology — Course Outline: MCQs

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Chemical pathology studies the biochemical changes in disease. It links clinical signs to laboratory tests, guiding diagnosis and management. Clinicians use these tests to confirm, stage, and monitor conditions.

sections.p: Chemical pathology is the analysis of body fluids and tissues for metabolic, hormonal, and toxic substances. Diagnosis relies on quantitative tests that reflect organ function or disease activity.

t.b: Renal function; high indicates impaired filtration
Liver injury; high suggests hepatocellular damage
Cardiac muscle injury; high confirms myocardial infarction
Glycaemic control over 3 months; high indicates diabetes
Coagulation status; prolonged indicates clotting factor deficiency or anticoagulant effect

sections.p: Severity is graded by laboratory thresholds and clinical context. Staging uses established systems such as the Child‑Pugh score for liver disease or the Ranson criteria for pancreatitis.
b: Use lab values to classify mild, moderate, severe

t.b: Predicts mortality in acute pancreatitis; >3 points = high risk
Assesses cirrhosis severity; higher points = worse prognosis

sections.p: Common causes vary by setting. In low‑resource areas, infections (HIV, TB, malaria, hepatitis B), nutritional deficiencies, and herbal toxins are frequent culprits.
Patients often show nonspecific symptoms: fatigue, jaundice, abdominal pain, or altered mental status. Lab abnormalities guide the differential.
b: Abdominal pain with lipase >3× ULN points to pancreatitis

sections.p: Tests answer specific pathophysiological questions. When unavailable, clinical judgment and alternative markers are used.
b: Use bedside tests when lab access is limited

t.b: Detects hypoglycaemia; low glucose = urgent treatment
Confirms parasitemia; positive = treat with antimalarial
Detects proteinuria; high protein suggests nephrotic syndrome

sections.p: Certain lab patterns predict imminent danger. Prompt recognition prevents mortality.
b: Markedly low platelets with bleeding → consumptive coagulopathy

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, then support organ function. Drug choice considers efficacy, safety, and local availability.
b: Anticoagulants for thrombotic events, avoiding bleeding risks

sections.p: Regular monitoring of key biomarkers assesses treatment response. Prevention focuses on vaccination, safe practices, and education.
b: Vaccinate against hepatitis B and influenza

sections.p: Some conditions mimic biochemical patterns; clinical context distinguishes them.
Certain factors can distort lab values, leading to misdiagnosis.

whenToSeekHelp: Acute renal failure with rising creatinine and oliguria
Markedly elevated liver enzymes with jaundice

faq.q: What is the most common cause of acute kidney injury in low‑resource settings?
faq.a: Severe dehydration from diarrhoea or malaria, and infections like leptospirosis.

faq.q: Why is HbA1c useful in diabetes management?
faq.a: It reflects average glucose over 2–3 months, guiding long‑term control.

faq.q: When should I order a liver function panel?
faq.a: Any patient with jaundice, abdominal pain, or unexplained fatigue.

exam: Explain how serum creatinine reflects glomerular filtration rate and its limitations in malnourished patients.
Describe the Ranson criteria for acute pancreatitis and how they guide treatment decisions.
Discuss the differential diagnosis of elevated AST/ALT and the role of viral serology.
